plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two side-by-side panels illustrating 2D translation as a geometric transformation in the xy-plane. In the left panel, an orange square at the origin is displaced to an upper-right position by a translation vector t, shown as a red arrow; the transformed square sits at coordinates (t_x, t_y) relative to the original. In the right panel, two successive translations are depicted: the square first moves by vector t to an intermediate position, then by vector s to a final position, with individual red arrows labeled t and s; a third red arrow labeled t+s connects the original square directly to the final position, demonstrating that the composition of two translations equals their vector sum. This figure establishes the additive composition rule for 2D translations, motivating their representation in homogeneous coordinates where composition reduces to matrix multiplication.

interactionPlan.concept: 2D translations compose by vector addition, which corresponds to matrix multiplication when represented in homogeneous coordinates.

Second translated orange square (draggable, visible in chained mode)

Red vector arrow 's' connecting the first square to the second square

interactions.teaches: Changing the translation vector directly updates the object's position and the corresponding displacement values in the homogeneous matrix.

interactions.label: Translation mode
interactions.teaches: Successive translations sum their displacement vectors, and this additive composition emerges naturally from multiplying their homogeneous matrices.

demo_steps.title: Single translation
demo_steps.narration: A translation displaces an object by vector t. Drag the translated square to change t and see how its components tx and ty are stored in the rightmost column of the homogeneous matrix.

demo_steps.title: Composing translations
demo_steps.narration: Applying a second translation s results in a net displacement of t + s. By using homogeneous coordinates, this geometric vector sum is perfectly captured by multiplying the two translation matrices.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Chaining translations adds their displacement vectors, and homogeneous coordinates allow this addition to be computed via standard matrix multiplication.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Consolidate the original two panels into a single interactive view. Draw a 2D Cartesian coordinate system with x (horizontal) and y (vertical) axes. Draw the original square fixed at the origin with an orange fill and black outline. Draw red vector arrows for 't', 's', and 't+s', labeling them near their midpoints. In 'Single' mode, only the first translation is visible; in 'Chained' mode, all three arrows and both translated squares are visible. Render the homogeneous matrices as live text formulas that update as the user drags the squares to change the vectors.

authoredContext:
Consider a translation by a 2D vector, $(t_x, t_y)$ as shown in
-translations. We'll denote the coordinates after the
transformation with a prime. In heterogeneous coordinates, we have
$$\begin{pmatrix}
 x' \\
 y' 
 \end{pmatrix}
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
 x \\
 y 
 \end{pmatrix}
 +
 \begin{pmatrix}
 t_x \\
 t_y 
 \end{pmatrix}
$$

(left) Translation. (right) Composition of two consecutive translations.

In summary, in homogeneous coordinates a translation becomes a product
with a matrix, and chaining translations can be done by multiplying the
matrices together. The benefits of using the homogeneous coordinates
will become more obvious later.

When chaining rotations and translations only we will have a euclidean
transformation (lengths and angles between lines are preserved). A
similarity transform is the result of chaining a rotation,
translation and scaling (with uniform scaling, $s_x=s_y$). In this case
angles are preserved but not lengths. Chaining all transformations
results in an affine transformation. Each set of transformations
forms a group.

In general, chaining translations, scalings, rotations and shears will
result in a generic matrix with the form: $$\mathbf{p}' = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
 a & b & c \\
 d & e & f \\
 0 & 0 & 1
 \end{bmatrix}
 \mathbf{p}$$ Any transformation with that form (6 degrees of
freedom) is an affine transformation. An affine transformation has the
property that parallel lines will remain parallel after the
transformation; however, lengths and non-zero angles might change.
